sources.news_title: Attorneys for Alaska say 'meritless' Trump demand to set aside ballots in Senate race 'not even possible'
sources.text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — Alaska's Republican-run state government on Saturday urged a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit filed at President Donald Trump's direction to stop the certification of a possible Democratic win in that state's pivotal U.S. Senate race, writing that there is “no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer.”
The scathing filing from the state's attorney general's office comes as U.S. District Court Judge Sharon L. Gleason set a deadline of Saturday for arguments over whether she should dismiss the lawsuit without even a hearing. The complaint from the U.S. Department of Justice has been roundly criticized by election law experts and demands that the judge halt certification of a possible win by Democrat Mary Peltola until it is determined whether voters were confused by the presence of a second candidate on the ballot with the same name as her main rival, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The Department of Justice on Friday added a request that the judge separate all ballots showing votes for the second Dan Sullivan until it can be determined whether voters were fooled into wasting their votes for a spoiler candidate. In its Saturday filing, Alaska said this was "both disturbing and impossible.” It added there would be no way to do that without violating voter privacy.
Trump also demanded that Peltola be prosecuted after The New York Times this week reported that internal texts and posts appear to show the Democrats' campaign was involved in recruiting the second Sullivan, a retired school teacher in the remote fishing village of Petersburg, onto the ballot. But the state filing notes that the two Sullivans are distinguished from each other on the ballot — the senator is listed as a Republican and the incumbent, while the other simply as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.”
“State officials carefully designed the ballot to minimize voter confusion,” Alaska officials wrote. “The Court should immediately dismiss this lawsuit with prejudice and allow state officials to conduct the general election — including ballot counting and certification — free from unwarranted federal interference.”
The Trump administration argued that a preamble to the 1990s law governing voter registration gave it the responsibility for ensuring states maintained the “integrity” of federal elections. It has said it’s simply trying to combat fraud by preventing the Democrat from being declared the victor in a race that could determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.
The Department of Justice issued a wave of subpoenas and announced it was conducting a criminal investigation in the case as the administration has stepped up its use of its legal powers to support Trump's side in the midterm election.
Peltola has denied involvement in the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot. The Times report was based on interviews with her former campaign manager, texts and contributions from a political group backing Peltola to an out-of-state Democratic consultant who recruited the second Sullivan.
Alaska’s Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, who announced a state probe into the situation after the Times story, has condemned the placement of the second Sullivan on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled this summer that the second candidate fulfilled all legal requirements to stay on. The state government’s filing on Saturday says that the new revelations about the possible role of Peltola’s campaign don’t change the fact that he’s legally on the ballot.
“Not every wrong can be righted in federal court,” the state wrote.
Peltola's campaign and voting rights groups also have urged Gleason to dismiss the case, putting them in unusual alignment with Alaska state officials.
“Imagine if the federal executive could pluck a few words like ‘election integrity’ from some statutory preamble and, on that basis alone, bend the machinery of state elections to his will, preemptively blocking certification of a U.S. Senate election to protect his preferred candidate from defeat and then subjecting voters to a law-enforcement-led inquest about who they ‘really’ supported,” the American Civil Liberties Union wrote in a filing urging the lawsuit's dismissal. “Imagine that world and ask whether it is what the Framers wanted or precisely what they most feared.”

sources.news_title: US Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots as criminal probe underway over Senate candidate
sources.text:
Anchorage, Alaska: The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska."
Separately, the Justice Department - as part of a lawsuit it filed last week - asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter "confusion" with the senator.
Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government "seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."
The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.
State elections officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot
Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot: "I am not interested in tricking voters," she said.
Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest.
The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a "substantial risk" that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy "will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity."
"To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary," the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.
Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation would be possible, writing that voters' ballots are comingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That's also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.
Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska's ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.
Timing of Justice Department announcements unusual
Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.
It's highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
Trump during a rally late Friday in Florida said Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan should be prosecuted. He noted U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche was in attendance and said, "He's going to make his own decision."
Trump, then addressing Blanche directly, said of decisions regarding the case, "Todd, please make your own," and watched Blanche's response.
Trump added: "OK, he said 'yes.'"
Peltola, at a campaign rally in Anchorage late Friday, said she is "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy." She said she doesn't need any help in winning the race outside of the support of voters.
Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times' reporting, that he'd ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.
Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.

sources.news_title: Trump administration accelerates Alaska Senate race probe | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Trump administration accelerates Alaska Senate race probe
WASHINGTON / ANCHORAGE >> President Donald Trump’s administration stepped up criminal and civil investigations into allegations that Democrats conspired to recruit a spoiler candidate in a critical Senate race in Alaska, U.S. officials said today, injecting fresh uncertainty into Tuesday’s congressional midterm election.
The Justice Department’s top prosecutor in Alaska, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a news conference that a Wednesday New York Times article about the effort had driven a “surge” of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place “intensely and swiftly.”
“Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they’re going to get one,” he said. “Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they’ll answer for it.”
Separately, the department today asked a federal judge to block Alaska from certifying the election results if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, also named Daniel Sullivan.
The contest between Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is widely seen as one of the few Senate races that could sway control of the chamber on Nov. 3.
A record 48 million people have cast early ballots, more than any other midterm election in U.S. history, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they intend to launch investigations into Trump’s administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against Iran.
If Democrats cannot flip the seat, their path to a majority narrows considerably, with the party needing to win at least two other races in mostly Republican states such as Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas. Trump’s fellow Republicans are likely to lose their slim majority in the U.S. House of Representatives, according to nonpartisan analysts.
The New York Times this week reported that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign arm helped recruit a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village who is named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr to appear on the ballot. Reuters has not been able to independently confirm the Times’ reporting.
Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also denied involvement. Sullivan, the retired teacher, has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken; both parties have engaged in “ballot stacking” by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents. Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted.
Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the investigation proceed. He also said the probe had been ongoing for months and that the Times report had added urgency to the investigation, but did not explain how.
Peltola’s campaign has asked a judge to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit, arguing it has no legal basis.
The Justice Department has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by noncitizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.
A U.S. appeals court today rejected the department’s request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week.
A lower court judge had already denied the administration’s request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters. California officials have said the Justice Department’s assertions relied on suspect data.
The administration’s legal moves represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the Constitution. Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington.
Trump has long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the U.S. is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found.
The president will campaign today in Florida, the latest in a series of rallies he has headlined in states he won handily in 2024 but where Democrats are now competitive, as he tries to stave off Republican losses on Tuesday.
Trump said today he would attend weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas after all, a day after canceling them, telling reporters at the White House that Republicans in those states had called him and asked him to reconsider.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated in the 2024 election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta today.
Additional reporting by Jarrett Renshaw, Nathan Layne, Jana Winter, Max Schwarz, Kia Johnson, Maria Tsvetkova, Doina Chiacu and Jan Wolfe.

sources.news_title: DOJ Moves to Halt Alaska Senate Certification Over Ballot Name Confusion
sources.text:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) asked a federal judge on Oct. 30 to block Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, saying votes cast for another candidate also named Dan Sullivan could alter the outcome.
Both state and federal criminal investigations are underway into an alleged scheme to place Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, on the ballot to draw votes away from the incumbent.
The DOJ argues in its lawsuit that Daniel J. Sullivan was brought into the race “to confuse voters,” and that the sole purpose of his candidacy “is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan.”
Peltola’s campaign, the DSCC, and Daniel J. Sullivan have denied any wrongdoing.
In court papers filed Oct. 30, the DOJ argues that a preliminary injunction should be granted because “monetary damages cannot compensate Alaskans duped into voting for Daniel J. Sullivan.”
“When voters are unable to fairly cast ballots in federal elections, the United States suffers irreparable harm,” the department said.
In the Oct. 30 filing, the DOJ recounted some of the Division of Elections’ findings.
The DOJ said that the state agency determined that Daniel J. Sullivan asked that the ballot show his name as “Dan S. Sullivan”—even though “S” is not his middle initial—it’s actually the incumbent’s initial.
The Division of Elections also found that Daniel J. Sullivan asked to be designated as a Republican on the ballot, even though he had never before “been affiliated with the Republican Party in Alaska,” the DOJ said. The agency held that Daniel J. Sullivan’s wish to change his party affiliation to match the incumbent’s, along with his desire to use a shortened version of his name that he had not previously used and that matched the incumbent’s name, “strongly suggests an intent to confuse [himself] with the incumbent Senator rather than to distinguish [himself] from him,” the DOJ said.
The DOJ also said that Daniel J. Sullivan “admitted in a July 18, 2026, interview with The New York Times that he voted for Democrats in the last three presidential elections and voted for Peltola when she ran for Congress.”
In its lawsuit, the DOJ is seeking a declaration that certifying any result affected by voter confusion would violate election officials’ duties under the National Voter Registration Act, as well as an injunction blocking certification in the specific scenario in which Sen. Sullivan loses but would have won if votes for Daniel J. Sullivan had been cast for him instead.
Meanwhile, state and federal investigations are underway.
Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for Alaska, told reporters on Oct. 30 that a federal criminal investigation has been moving forward for several months, but the Oct. 28 New York Times report on Peltola’s campaign has led to a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”
“We will work closely with our partners at the Alaska Department of Law to ensure that the facts are thoroughly examined and that anyone found to have violated state law is held accountable,” McDaniel said.

sources.news_title: Justice Department requests separating Alaska ballots that rank Dan J. Sullivan in Senate race
sources.text:
The Trump administration asked a federal judge Friday to issue an order before Monday directing Alaska election officials to segregate all ballots ranking Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan as it continues its investigation into his candidacy.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote in a court filing that state officials should “preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary.”
“These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration,” he added.
The filing did not spell out a process for ballot review or explain how reviewing a ballot would show if a voter was confused about ranking the candidates. Alaska uses ranked choice voting, and there are four Senate candidates on the ballot.
The Trump administration has ramped up its efforts to inject itself into the Alaska election, which by statute is handled by state officials, after The New York Times reported this week that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a former school teacher, to run against Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Peltola has denied any involvement in Sullivan’s campaign.
At a campaign rally Friday evening, Peltola told supporters that she was “so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else’s candidacy.”
“I want fewer candidates in the primary. I’m not out soliciting more competition,” Peltola said. “I know we can beat Dan Sullivan because every step of the way, even before I got in this race, my poll numbers were higher than his.”
Peltola urged her supporters to get out to vote and encourage those around them, warning that some voters may have been discouraged from voting for her due to the allegations.
“Our work isn’t done yet because we know that there are people out there who have not voted, who don’t have a plan to vote, who are so turned off by the smear campaigns and the garbage, and you know the accusations, the hollow accusations,” she said. “It’s really up to us to remind people why we need to get out and vote.”
Woodward, alongside Alaska’s top federal prosecutor, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, made three other filings Friday regarding the civil case the administration is pursuing in hopes of blocking Alaska from certifying the Senate election results.
In one filing, the prosecutors requested expedited sharing of “internal and external conversations” from Peltola’s campaign “regarding its efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.” Another filing asks for the “Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s internal and external conversations regarding its efforts recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.”
The DSCC has said it was “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
An additional filing seeks a preliminary injunction in the case.

Friday’s filings came shortly after Heyman held a press conference in Alaska, where he acknowledged a parallel criminal case.

Asked what potential crimes prosecutors are looking into, Heyman declined to provide details.
“Because this is an ongoing investigative matter, we can’t discuss the specifics of those investigative steps, and who or may or may not be involved,” he said. “This protects the integrity of the investigation and it protects those who may be the subject or target of those investigations.”
Heyman cited the recent reporting from The New York Times, saying the “new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”
The Justice Department issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests as of Thursday, including subpoenas sent to the campaign offices of Peltola and of Dan J. Sullivan.
President Donald Trump, who has urged legal action against Peltola and the second Sullivan, said Friday morning that he doesn’t know whether Sen. Dan S. Sullivan can win with the current ballot.
“I will tell you, he’s a great senator, and what they tried to do, and he would, you know, he would have won,” Trump said in an interview with Kansas City talk radio host Pete Mundo. “I don’t know how he can win here because you’re splitting up the vote illegally. I think it’s a total fraud.”
Trump has said repeatedly that Dan J. Sullivan should be removed from the ballot.
In an interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity earlier this week, Sen. Sullivan told supporters in Alaska how to mark up their ballot to best help him on Election Day.
“So rank me first, Sullivan, Dan S. Registered Republican incumbent. That’s what the ballot says,” he said. “Rank the other Republican second, [Gerald] Heikes. Rank, I hate to say it, Sean, but in our screwed-up system, you rank the fake guy third, and then of course blank. Do not rank Peltola. Now that is the screwed up system we have.”

sources.news_title: Feds Target Alleged Voter Deception Plot in Heated Alaska Senate Showdown
sources.text:
Federal authorities are taking an extraordinary look at the fiercely contested United States Senate race in Alaska. The controversy began when a retired teacher from Petersburg, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., entered the race. He shares a nearly identical name with the incumbent Republican Senator, Dan S. Sullivan. Under the unique Alaska primary system, the top four vote-getters advance to the general election. In the August primary, former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola finished first. Incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan placed second, while the Petersburg challenger finished third with 2.5 percent of the vote. Republican Gerald Heikes also advanced to the final ballot after a fourth-place Democratic candidate withdrew from the contest.
Republicans quickly raised alarms that having two candidates named Dan Sullivan would confuse voters in a tight race. They alleged that Democratic operatives orchestrated a decoy campaign to siphon votes away from the incumbent senator. State officials pushed back against those claims after the Alaska Supreme Court upheld the challenger’s right to run. The state elections division noted that the ballot clearly distinguishes the incumbent Republican from the unaligned challenger. Meanwhile, the Petersburg candidate has repeatedly insisted that his campaign is genuine and not meant to trick anyone.
Despite state assurances, the Department of Justice escalated the matter into both civil and criminal territories. On the civil side, federal attorneys filed a lawsuit seeking to block election certification if voter confusion alters the outcome. State attorneys argue the federal lawsuit has no legal basis and intrudes upon state authority. Alongside the civil litigation, federal prosecutors have widened a criminal probe into how the challenger’s campaign was formed. Investigators are scrutinizing recent media reports alleging that Democratic campaign groups helped recruit and fund the namesake candidate.
United States Attorney Michael J. Heyman and FBI Anchorage Special Agent in Charge Matthew Schlegel addressed the matter Friday. During a joint press conference, Heyman warned that anyone who illegally deceives voters will answer for their actions. Heyman and Schlegel emphasized that federal investigators are reviewing both civil and criminal aspects of the alleged ballot scheme. Preserving ballots and election records remains a central focus as the Department of Justice seeks expedited discovery in court. Voters who have questions about ballot layout or official procedures can consult the state division of elections for guidance.

sources.news_title: Top federal prosecutor in Alaska says criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate
sources.text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
The dueling developments came days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”
Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter “confusion” with the senator.
Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government “seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary.”
The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.
State elections officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot
Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot. Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest.
The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a “substantial risk” that Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy “will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity.”
“To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary,” the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.
Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation was possible, writing that voters’ ballots are comingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn’t segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn’t reveal any voter’s reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That’s also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.
Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska’s ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.
Timing of Justice Department announcements unusual
Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.
It’s highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
At a campaign event in Juneau late Thursday, Peltola began her speech by saying she wanted to “clear the air.”
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about,” Peltola said. “I am not interested in tricking voters.”
Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times’ reporting, that he’d ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.
Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.
___
Durkin Richer reported from Washington. Bohrer reported from Juneau, Alaska.

sources.news_title: Trump administration accelerates criminal probe into Alaska Senate race
sources.text:
Trump administration accelerates criminal probe into Alaska Senate race
ANCHORAGE, Alaska – President Donald Trump’s administration stepped up criminal and civil investigations into allegations that Democrats conspired to recruit a spoiler candidate in a critical Senate race in Alaska, officials said on Friday, injecting fresh uncertainty into Tuesday’s midterm elections.
The top federal prosecutor in Alaska, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a news conference that a Wednesday New York Times article about the effort had driven a “surge” of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place “intensely and swiftly.”
“Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they’re going to get one,” he said. “Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they’ll answer for it.”
The Alaska contest is widely seen as one of the U.S. Senate races that could sway control of the chamber, now narrowly held by Trump’s Republicans.
Trump ordered suit, claims ‘fraud
at highest level’
The Justice Department’s legal actions in Alaska and California, where the Trump administration is trying to prevent some ballots from being counted, represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the U.S. Constitution.
When the DOJ filed the civil suit against Alaska a week ago, Trump told reporters, “I’m the one that said do it.”
Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the Alaska investigation proceed, although Trump has called for a prosecution of Senate candidate Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
“This is voter fraud at the highest level,” Trump told a Florida rally on Friday.
The Department of Justice asked a federal judge on Friday to ensure the preservation of ballots that “may be impacted by voter confusion.” The court filing requested the judge’s help obtaining documents from the Democratic campaign and others to determine “whether Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy is frivolous or fraudulent.”
The DOJ also has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken. Both parties have engaged in “ballot stacking” by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents.
If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they intend to launch investigations of the Trump administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against Iran.
The New York Times reported this week that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign arm helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village, to appear on the ballot. Reuters has not independently confirmed the Times’ reporting.
Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also denied involvement. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
Surge of voting nationwide despite uncertainty
Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further disruptions from the Trump administration, which has sued about 30 states seeking unredacted voter rolls.
“The new tactic is just to create enough confusion and enough uncertainty and enough doubt through the filing of all these lawsuits to lay the groundwork to ultimately, I think, challenge the results once the dust settles after Tuesday,” said Jonathan Diaz, of the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center.
Trump has long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the U.S. is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found.
Despite any uncertainty, a record 49 million people have cast early ballots, more than any other midterm election in U.S. history, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail.
The DOJ has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by noncitizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.
A U.S. appeals court on Friday rejected the department’s request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week.
A lower court judge had denied the administration’s request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters.
Trump said on Friday he would attend weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, a day after canceling them, telling reporters at the White House that Republicans in those states had called him and asked him to reconsider.

sources.news_title: Simultaneous civil and criminal investigations launched over Alaska Dem ballot-stacking allegations
sources.text:
Simultaneous civil and criminal investigations launched over Alaska Dem ballot-stacking allegations
The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed Friday that both a civil and criminal investigation have begun into allegations of Democratic efforts to recruit a man named Dan Sullivan to run against the existing incumbent Republican senator to potentially confuse voters.
Big picture view:
U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman for the district of Alaska held a news conference saying a preliminary injunction would be filed on the civil side for "expedited discovery" by Monday to freeze ballots and assess voter deception, just a day before the election.
"Every Alaskan deserves a fair election and they’re going to get one," Heyman told reporters, adding that recent reporting from The New York Times revealed "troubling new revelations."
Heyman said the pair of investigations were occurring "simultaneously and within their own lanes."
"The civil lawsuit is publicly faced and is focused on preserving the ballots versus the criminal investigation on the other side," he said. The civil investigation is focused on protecting ballots under the National Voter Registration Act.
The backstory:
Alaska's ballot for the U.S. Senate seat will feature incumbent Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, a former U.S. House member for Alaska, a retired teacher whose name is also Daniel Sullivan, and a fourth long-shot candidate.
Earlier this week, a report from the New York Times claimed Peltola's aides worked with the campaign's lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats' campaign arm to recruit the retired teacher, known as Dan J. Sullivan, to run.
Voters wait in line to cast their ballots past a "Polling Place Here" sign at a polling location inside the Midtown Mall during early voting for the midterm election in Anchorage, Alaska, US, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. The Trump administration is sui
The retiree has denied allegations that Democrats asked him to run and said he has had "zero, none, zilch" contact with Peltola’s campaign.
Last week, the Trump administration asked a federal court to block certification of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses the election. The lawsuit, filed Oct. 22 by the Department of Justice, argues the state should be barred from certifying a Democratic win if Daniel J. Sullivan, a previously unknown candidate, is allowed to stay on the ballot. DOJ lawyers say federal law obligates states to safeguard the integrity of federal elections.
The race is considered pivotal in the GOP battle to keep Senate control. Though Daniel J. Sullivan entered the race without a party designation, Republicans have accused him of being a Democratic plant intended to siphon votes from the incumbent.
Alaska does have a ranked-choice voting system which does allow voters to select both candidates on a ballot if they are confused.
What they're saying:
Heyman said Alaskan voters should vote for who they intend to support and that officials are "working to make sure it counts how you intended."
Heyman said when credible information comes out they will act on it, and they’ve already received a number of new pieces of information in the last few hours.
"We will not let anyone or any group undermine this election," he stressed.
Former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, who is running for Senate, has denied allegations that she tried to recruit an Alaskan citizen named Dan Sullivan to run against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, her main rival.
"I just want to clear the air," she said at a campaign rally in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."
But some legal experts have said the Justice Department’s lawsuit is weak because the U.S. Constitution delegates the responsibility for administering elections to state governments rather than the federal government. University of Kentucky law professor Joshua Douglas told Reuters that claims that Democrats helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to serve as a "spoiler" in the race likely would not help the Justice Department’s case.
"Regardless of who encouraged him to run, the second Dan Sullivan validly qualified for the ballot. And this is a matter of state law," Douglas said.
Peltola's campaign lawyers have asked U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the Justice Department's lawsuit, arguing the federal government lacks the required legal authority to bring the case.
What's next:
It is not clear how soon Gleason might decide on whether to dismiss the lawsuit. However, that decision could come as early as Saturday.
Early voting continues through Monday, depending on the voting district; some areas allow voting on Saturday and Sunday.
Election Day is Tuesday.
The Source: Information for this story came from the Associated Press, Reuters, the Alaska Division of Elections and previous FOX News reporting. This story was reported from Orlando.

Federal prosecutor in Alaska confirms criminal investigation into Senate Dem nominee is underway
The investigation comes after Mary Peltola denied Thursday that she had any knowledge of the effort to put another Dan Sullivan on the ballot alongside incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The feds' top prosecutor in Alaska confirmed Friday that the Justice Department is investigating allegations of a plot to confuse voters in the midterms by recruiting a candidate with the same name as the state's incumbent senator.
U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman said the investigation has been going on for a while, but the confirmation comes after The New York Times reported this week that Alaska Senate Democratic nominee Mary Peltola's campaign helped recruit a retiree named Dan J. Sullivan to run against Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in next week's elections.
The attorney said the new information resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” according to the Associated Press.
“When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information to deceive voters and we will act on it. We are acting on it intensely and swiftly,” Heyman said.
The investigation also comes after Peltola denied Thursday that she had any knowledge of the effort to put the other Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“I just want to clear the air,” she said. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

sources.news_title: Alaska Senate election: DOJ wants to 'segregate' all ballots for 2nd Sullivan candidate
sources.text:
The Department of Justice wants "to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking" a candidate named Dan Sullivan for a potential investigation of whether voters in Alaska's U.S. Senate election mistakenly ranked him in the belief he was incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, a federal prosecutor told a judge in a court filing late Friday.
The filing came in a lawsuit by the DOJ, which asks District Court Judge Sharon Gleason to block state election officials from immediately certifying the Senate election if Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that might be attributable to voter confusion from the presence of the other Sullivan on the ballot. The DOJ wants to conduct an investigation to determine voter intent if the incumbent loses.
"Election Day is on November 3, 2026, which poses a substantial risk that the candidacy before us will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity," U.S. Attorney for Alaska Michael Heyman said in the filing, signed by one of his assistant prosecutors.
"The United States of America contends that the proposed precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, showing good cause for expedited consideration," the filing said.
Heyman earlier Friday told reporters at a press conference that there is an "ongoing" criminal investigation into how and why retired school teacher Dan Sullivan decided to run for the Senate for the first time this year.
The DOJ's suit, which President Donald Trump said he had requested, claims the "sole purpose" of the non-incumbent Sullivan running was to benefit the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola by reducing the number of votes for Sen. Sullivan.
"We will not let anyone or any group undermine this election," said Heyman at a press conference in Anchorage, which was held just four days before Election Day.
"There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that is ongoing," Heyman said. "There is a surge of FBI resources and resources in this office."
"Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they're going to get one," the prosecutor said.
He said that the criminal probe has been underway for months. Heyman had previously recused himself from the probe because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, but that recusal was rescinded Thursday because he was no longer under consideration.
Heyman said the criminal investigation has been accelerated because of a New York Times report on Wednesday that said aides Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee helped recruit the retired teacher to enter the Senate race with the hope of drawing votes from the incumbent Sullivan.
"When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information … and we will act on it," Heyman said.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny being involved in the retiree's Senate campaign.
Heyman, when questioned by reporters, would not say what criminal statute might have been violated
Earlier Friday, a federal judge kept on a fast track efforts to dismiss the DOJ's suit.
Judge Sharon Gleason ordered the DOJ to respond by 1 p.m. Alaska Time to the new dismissal motions, which were filed hours after the department amended its suit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage on Thursday to add a new legal claim.
The DOJ's updating of the civil complaint forced Gleason to rule the prior dismissal motions were moot.
Gleason gave state election officials, the campaign of Democratic nominee and other groups until noon Saturday to reply to the DOJ's response.
The judge's order leaves open the possibility that she will rule on the dismissal motions before Tuesday, which is Election Day, as both the state and Peltola's campaign have requested.
The state, the campaign, and other intervenors in the suit argue the DOJ has no legal authority to block certification of an election because two candidates on a four-candidate ballot happen to share the same name.
The winner of Alaska's race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate starting in January. Republicans currently have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.
Alaska's election uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate obtains more than 50% of the vote in the first count, then the fourth-place finisher will be eliminated, and the second choice on that candidate's ballots will be allocated to the remaining candidates.
Only Peltola and Sen. Sullivan are considered likely to draw large shares of the votes.
The DOJ's suit seeks to delay certification of the Senate election if Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion over the presence of the other candidate, who is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot.
The amended complaint, which updates the suit filed Oct. 23, added a claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim, under the National Voter Registration Act.
It also contained added details from the Times article.
Peltola's campaign, in its dismissal motion filed Thursday, said, "Rather than defend its indefensible legal claims as it was ordered to do, the Department of Justice ... has filed an Amended Complaint that does nothing to address the fatal problems that preclude it from bringing this case or obtaining the relief that it seeks."
"The U.S. Constitution leaves the regulation of federal elections exclusively to the States and to Congress, and DOJ has no statutory authority to bring this case," the motion said.
In their own dismissal motion, state election officials said the amended lawsuit "rests on the same meritless theory that the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — a voter registration law — governs this case, which has nothing to do with voter registration."
"Because this reading of the NVRA fails, the amended complaint fails," the motion said.

sources.news_title: Three things can be true at once in Alaska #ELB
sources.text:
The last week has been fairly remarkable in Alaska, but I wanted to put down a few thoughts together and show how three different things can all be true at once: there were good reasons to exclude the second Sullivan from the ballot; even if Alaska didn’t do so, there are good reasons to think voters won’t be confused because of mitigating steps taken; and even if voters aren’t confused, there are still very real criminal charges to consider in this case, and further investigation is essential to determine whether they should be brought.
First, there were good reasons for the state to exclude Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. from the ballot in June. As I wrote then, there was certainly no federal constitutional bar in doing so. And the facts, even as we knew them then, suggested his candidacy was not bona fide:
When Dan J. filed his notice of candidacy, he claimed his name was “Dan S. Sullivan.” “S.” is not Dan J.’s middle initial, but the middle initial of the incumbent. No explanation is given as to this “error,” and the trial court characterized this as an “understandable concern” that was “quickly corrected.” It seems odd that the trial court failed to credit the elections director’s finding on this–it hardly seems to be a random mistake.
Excluding candidates who engage in deception in their efforts to appear on the ballot is hardly new. When a woman changed her name to Carol Moseley Braun, then later attempted to appear on the ballot, Illinois kicked her off. Name changes are, of course, an extreme version of this problem.
The elections director identified other reasons to doubt the legitimacy of the candidacy–including mimicking the incumbent Senator’s design and color scheme in a website, metadata in electronic filings that included the name of a Democratic consultant, no previous affiliation with the Republican Party, and others.
I admitted I had “less certainty” there about state legal authority to do so. And perhaps that’s what the Alaska Supreme Court concluded.
But, unfortunately, the Alaska Supreme Court has yet to issue its list of reasons. On June 29, it posted this:
The 6/26/2026 order of the superior court directing the Division to include appellee Sullivan as a candidate for United States Senator on the primary election ballot is AFFIRMED. This matter is remanded for the Division of Elections to determine, in the first instance, how appellee Sullivan shall be listed as a candidate within the confines of existing Alaska ballot design law. A full opinion will be issued at a later date.
It would be helpful to know (1) whether it included him because of a mistaken interpretation of federal law, in which case certiorari to the United States Supreme Court would have been appropriate; (2) whether it included him because state law prevented the elections director from investigating whether a candidate was bona fide, a matter largely left untouched by intervening events; or (3) whether it included him because it concluded the elections director made a mistake of fact, in which case recent events could call into question its decision.
Second, the elections division has minimized the risk of voter confusion through its ballot labeling process, and there is no federal claim to prevent certification of the election. The elections division did an admirable job reducing voter confusion by including very clear distinguishing marks on the ballot between the candidates (a matter, apparently, that Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. never attempted to preserve in litigation). The elections division (1) distinguished “Dan” from “Daniel”; (2) included middle initials, (3) added “Jr.” to the alternative candidate, (4) put “Registered Republican” next to Dan S. Sullivan and nothing next to Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.; and (5) added “incumbent” next to Dan S. Sullivan.
If there were no intention to confuse voters (more on that in my third point), but if this were a mere happenstance of two people named John Smith on the ballot, these are the very distinguishing markers a chief election official would use to reduce confusion. And, of course, ranked choice voting can help–if voters rank the Sullivans next to each other in any order will, in the vast majority of circumstances, not affect anything. And the primary election results suggested few voters were confused. (I also doubt the Senate would refuse to seat a candidate because of the ballot here, and of course the facts such as a wide margin of victory could mitigate any such concerns, too.)
Given all of this effort to reduce confusion, there should be little reason to contest the election after the fact under state law. And certainly there’s no reason to do so under federal law. The federal lawsuit I derided earlier as “one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen” remains true. Just because the facts are stronger doesn’t mean the legal claim improves–because the legal claim is nonexistent. The amended complaint adds a Supremacy Clause argument, but, of course, the Supremacy Clause works when you can cite an underlying federal law or some more general displacement, which doesn’t exist here.
Third, there are real reasons for a preliminary criminal investigation after the New York Times report. I have been hesitant on this front and continue to wonder what might happen, so these are only tentative thoughts. To start, I have emphasized in some commentary that the process is really left to the voters and the political process now, not to litigation, as to the validity of the election. I think that’s still true. Much of the deception, intentional or not, has been rightfully mitigated.
I do wonder if there were campaign finance violations committed here. We’ll have to wait and see how contributions were structured, and whether some where appropriately made but simply difficult to find in the disclosure data, or whether some were in violation of law.
But I also want to offer some greater hesitation and suggest that other criminal violations might still be on the table. Rick H. offers some helpful thoughts on this front earlier this week, but I think some additional facts might complicate the analysis.
If the facts are what they appear to be–a small group of people tried to find someone with the same name as the incumbent Republican in an effort to get that name on the ballot for the purpose of confusing voters and trying to get voters to miscast votes–that, to me, is a serious problem.
It is different in kind from some of the practices Rick H. rightly describes as fairly common, e.g., “Republicans boosting Greens and Democrats boosting Libertarians.” I am less sure it is just “more extreme” and more wonder if it is different in kind. Yes, pushing Cornel West, Kanye West, Jill Stein, or whatever other candidate to appear on the ballot is designed, in some instances, to get voters to cast a vote for someone else. But it is not designed to confuse their support. The similarity of name is, as part of this process, expressly deceptive. And to me, that puts it more closely to telling voters the wrong date or time or location of the election–it is an effort to confuse voters and prevent them from exercising a choice.
To the extent there is a right to vote for Senators under the Seventeenth Amendment, there is a plausible case to be made that a conspiracy (even if a failed one) to deceive voters as to which candidate to vote for through confusion of candidates’ names on the ballot, one that could rise to a conspiracy to deprive voters of their rights. (And it’s possible there are related provisions of state law.)
To draw a different metaphor: recall the “butterfly ballots” in Florida in 2000. Recall how it appeared some voters might have been confused by the format and accidentally voted for Pat Buchanan instead of Al Gore. Now, suppose, instead, some election administrator had intentionally designed the ballot to operate that way. One would, I think, rightly wonder if this effort to confuse voters–even if the voters could read carefully and mark their ballots appropriately–should be free from criminal investigation.
One useful case note to consider. A similar type of dispute arose in Indiana in a Democratic primary in Gary, Indiana in 1983, over two candidates named Grimes. While the Seventh Circuit ultimately rejected a finding of a conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (finding no race-based animus), it did have this to say:
As the district court noted, the effects of this fraud could have been avoided if the voters had read the ballot “with a modicum of care.” Appellees thus argue that there can be no interference with the plaintiffs’ right to vote, because the Constitution “does not protect the right to vote blindly.” We reject this argument as patently absurd under these facts. The jury found that the defendants conspired to place John Grimes on the ballot in order to confuse the supporters of Douglas Grimes. What the defendants are essentially arguing is that there can be no recovery for the plaintiffs, because only “negligent” voters were taken in by the scheme. Our response to this disingenuous position parallels that of the district court. . . . As the district court stated, “Their right to vote might be seriously impaired if they had no legal protection against attempts to mislead them, even though more alert and informed voters would not be misled.”
It’s why I think Rick H. can be right that a “conspiracy” would fail for purposes of the National Vote Registration Act preamble that the Department of Justice cites in its lawsuit, but that, in my view, it is more plausible to succeed for something else. As Grimes notes elsewhere, it is a highly sensitive inquiry to inquire into sham candidates (UPDATE: and, to be sure, there may be real First Amendment defenses). That said, I think there is more to be said here about criminal investigation for those who induced the candidacy, much more so than the candidate himself (at this stage, anyway).
This is, of course, all highly tentative. I’d want to think more about where that line from “ordinary politics” and “dirty tricks” crosses into behavior that is designed to prevent voters from exercising a choice. On the facts, as I note here, I think the voters have been appropriately informed, and there is little likelihood of actual confusion. But I think the attempts to do so this spring and summer could still be criminal.
This is not a conclusion that should be reached lightly, of course. Meaningful due process exists in criminal cases for a reason, and drawing this line is, inevitably, a difficult one. More evidence–perhaps more comes out in subpoenas or in text messages that the New York Times didn’t report on–may come out and help move the case in one direction or another. But it’s something I’ll be watching in the weeks ahead.

sources.news_title: The Latest: Justice Department looks to separate Alaska ballots that rank Dan J. Sullivan
As Alaskans vote, state’s top federal prosecutor confirms criminal investigation of Dem groups
sources.text:
As Alaskans vote, state’s top federal prosecutor confirms criminal investigation of Dem groups
A civil lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections is also continuing in federal court, with a ruling possible before Monday
U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman for the District of Alaska speaks at an Oct. 30, 2026, news conference about U.S. Justice Department investigations into the Alaska U.S. Senate race. Next to him is Col. Maurice Hughes of the Alaska State Troopers. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
The U.S. Department of Justice has launched criminal and civil investigations into groups affiliated with the U.S. Senate campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, Alaska’s top federal prosecutor confirmed Friday during a news conference with reporters.
Michael Heyman, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska, said there has been “a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska” since the New York Times published an article describing how Democratic campaigners sought to recruit spoiler candidates who could siphon votes away from incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, who is running for re-election.
Heyman said the investigation has been ongoing for months but the Times article gave it new momentum.
One of the people allegedly recruited by the campaigners was independent Dan J. Sullivan, who is on the election ballot alongside the incumbent, Peltola and Republican Gerald Heikes.
Despite repeated questions, Heyman did not say what law the Peltola-affiliated groups are being accused of breaking.
Recruiting a spoiler candidate isn’t against the law unless accompanied by some other violation, such as lying to a court or offering a bribe to a candidate.
“I mean, you’re assuming that there is a crime being committed. It’s a criminal investigation, right? And that’s what we do — we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I’m not going to comment on what those theories are, and I’m also not going to put the cart before the horse,” he said.
Heyman also declined to say who is being investigated by federal officials.
Speaking Thursday night in Juneau, Peltola said she was unaware of the recruitment effort, denying one element of the Times reporting.
Peltola’s campaign organization, Alaskans for Mary, has also denied involvement, but the Times article describes events before that group’s creation and also said an intermediary did much of the recruiting.
Separately from the federal criminal investigation, Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a state-level criminal investigation by the Alaska Department of Public Safety. That agency also declined to say who is being investigated and what law might have been broken.
In civil court, the Department of Justice has sued the Alaska Division of Elections and has asked U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason — an appointee of President Barack Obama — to prevent the state from declaring anyone but Dan S. Sullivan the winner of the U.S. Senate election.
That could allow time for further investigation, federal attorneys argued, and on Friday, they filed a motion asking a judge to order the Division of Elections to preserve all ballots cast for Dan S. Sullivan.
The Division of Elections promptly responded that it already preserves federal ballots for 22 months.
The federal government also asked Gleason to order the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — two groups linked by the New York Times to the recruitment effort — to turn over related text messages and other communications.
The Times relied on text messages provided by a former Peltola campaign manager when reporting its article.
That request may not matter — Gleason is expected to first rule on whether or not the Department of Justice is allowed to bring its lawsuit at all. The U.S. Constitution prescribes that states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections except where provided by Congress.
The federal government has offered a legally tenuous argument stating that the introduction to the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 gives the federal government a general interest in elections, but that argument has been opposed by the Division of Elections, Democratic groups, nonpartisan groups that have intervened in the lawsuit, the NAACP and other experts offering legal advice to the court.
Gleason has indicated that she will rule no later than Monday on whether or not the federal government has standing.
Some outside experts believe the legal actions in Alaska are part of a broader campaign by the administration of President Donald Trump to disrupt a possible Democratic wave in the ongoing general election.
National polling indicates Democratic candidates may perform significantly better than normal in races across the country during this year’s midterm elections.
Alaska’s Senate race is one of a handful that may decide whether Democrats or Republicans control the U.S. Senate. If control of the Senate comes down to Alaska and Peltola wins but is denied the opportunity to take office, it could preserve Republican control for weeks or months longer than normal.
This week, Dunleavy declined to say whether he would certify Peltola the winner of the election if she received the most votes.
Last week, Trump said he had ordered the Department of Justice to file the civil complaint against the Division of Elections.
On Friday, a CNN reporter asked Heyman if he had spoken with the White House about the criminal or civil investigation.
“I have not had any discussions with the White House about those complaints,” Heyman said.
Speaking Oct. 13 at a rally in Wasilla, Trump told a crowd that he had just met with Heyman.
“I told him — I just shook his hand, took a picture — I said I hope you’re going to make sure there’s no cheating, because any place you have rank(ed) choice, you have damn bad cheating. And we can’t let that happen. So, we’re going to defend the integrity of Alaska’s elections,” Trump said.
Speaking to reporters on Friday in Anchorage, Heyman said, “This is all about election integrity. I want to encourage everyone with information on whether it be the information that we know about the Dan Sullivan issue or any other election integrity issue, to contact the FBI.”

sources.news_title: DOJ seeks to isolate Alaska ballots as criminal probe underway over Senate candidate
sources.text:
ANCHORAGE — The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska."
Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter "confusion" with the senator.
Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government "seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."
The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.
State elections officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot
Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot. Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest.
The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a "substantial risk" that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy "will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity."
"To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary," the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.
Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation was possible, writing that voters' ballots are comingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That's also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.
Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska's ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.
Timing of Justice Department announcements unusual
Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.
It's highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
At a campaign event in Juneau late Thursday, Peltola began her speech by saying she wanted to "clear the air."
"I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about," Peltola said. "I am not interested in tricking voters."
Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times' reporting, that he'd ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.
Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.
___
Durkin Richer reported from Washington. Bohrer reported from Juneau.
